request.state: For over a century, global production has been dominated by the Haber–Bosch process, which catalytically combines N2 and H2 under extreme temperatures (400–650 °C) and pressures (200–400 atm).^1 Consequently, this energy-intensive process accounts for approximately [[2%]] of global energy consumption and 1.8% of global CO2 emissions, primarily due to the steam-reforming of methane for H2 production.^2 Despite its high energy efficiency at large-scale production, the process still relies on centralized, continuous operations, presenting a signicant barrier to inte-grating intermittent renewable energy sources.
